Something important about tanzanite

Tanzanite is relatively soft (6–7 on the Mohs scale) and can be damaged by knocks. This matters for an engagement ring worn every day. I'd favour:

A protective halo or bezel setting.
A low-profile design rather than a tall, exposed solitaire.
Platinum or 18ct gold.
A gemstone certificate or independent appraisal.
A good returns policy and a written warranty.

I'd also ask for actual photographs or video of the exact stone in daylight, rather than relying on heavily enhanced website photographs.

Yes! Etsy can be a good place to buy a genuine sapphire ring, including beautiful natural sapphire and vintage rings. However, I'd be careful because Etsy is a marketplace made up of individual sellers, not a specialist jeweller.

There are genuine, reputable gemstone sellers on Etsy, but there are also listings where:

A synthetic (lab-created) sapphire is advertised simply as a sapphire.

A glass or imitation stone is described misleadingly.

A treated sapphire is sold without clearly explaining the treatment.

The photographs look much better than the actual ring.

The important thing is knowing exactly what you're buying.

My checklist before buying on Etsy

I'd only buy if the seller can confirm all of these:

Natural or lab-grown? Ask explicitly for a natural, earth-mined sapphire if that's what you want.

Treatment: Is it untreated, heat-treated or diffusion-treated? Heat treatment is common and isn't necessarily a bad thing.

Certificate: For an expensive ring, ask for an independent gemmological report confirming the stone is natural. GIA is one option.

Metal: Check whether it's solid 9ct, 14ct or 18ct gold, rather than gold-plated.

Reviews: Look for reviews with customer photos, not just star ratings.

Returns: Make sure you can return it if an independent jeweller finds the sapphire isn't as described.

My biggest piece of advice

Don't be put off by a heat-treated natural sapphire. That's very common. But don't pay natural sapphire prices for a lab-created stone.

What to look for when buying a ruby
This is particularly important for an engagement ring because it will hopefully be worn every day.

Main risks

Generally, a specialist is the better bet for colored gemstones, though it depends on what you’re buying and how much you’re spending.

Why specialists tend to win
- Selection and sourcing. Specialists often buy directly from cutters or mines, so you can compare many stones of the same type and see real differences in color, clarity, and cut. Chains usually carry a narrow, pre-selected range.
- Expertise. Colored stones are far more variable than diamonds. Origin, treatments (heat, oil, diffusion, irradiation), and color saturation all affect value heavily, and a good specialist can explain these. Chain staff are often trained mainly on diamonds and sales.
- Disclosure. Reputable specialists are upfront about treatments and will often provide lab reports from labs like GIA, AGL, Gübelin, or SSEF for higher-value stones.
- Pricing. With fewer layers of overhead and brand markup, you often get better quality for the money, especially for stones in the mid-to-high range.

When a chain can make sense
- You want a lower-priced piece (say, a simple birthstone ring) and care more about convenience than stone quality.
- You value a standardized return policy, warranty, or financing.

Styles you’ll see

Gold purity

14k is harder and more durable, so it suits everyday wear. It also has a slightly paler yellow tone.
18k has a richer, warmer color and a higher gold content. It’s a bit softer, though that matters little for studs.
10k is the most affordable and the toughest, but its color is lighter.

Ruby quality

Look for a vivid red, ideally with a slight hint of blue (often called “pigeon’s blood” at the top end). Very dark or orangey stones are less valued.
Most rubies are heat-treated, which is standard and accepted. Untreated stones cost much more, and a lab report is worth asking for.
Lab-created rubies look the same as natural ones and cost far less, so they’re a good option if you want a larger or more flawless stone on a budget.

Practical tips

Screw-back or locking friction backs are safer for expensive stones.
Total carat weight (ctw) covers both earrings. For example, 0.30 ctw means about 0.15 ct per ear.

What the law requires

In the US, FTC guidelines require disclosure of any enhancement that dramatically affects a gemstone’s value, and whether the treatment is permanent. Heating is treated differently. Look for plain wording such as “heated,” “no indications of heating,” “filled,” “oiled” or “treatment unknown.” If a listing says nothing at all, ask before buying.

Specialists generally focus heavily on loose stones, unique sourcing, and bespoke designs.

Variable Consistency: Quality and customer service standards can fluctuate wildly between different independent shops.

When it comes to officially certifying and grading gemstones, legitimacy depends entirely on the independent gemological laboratory that analyzed the stone. A valid certificate is never issued by the jeweler or the seller themselves; it must come from a recognized, unbiased third-party scientific institution.

The industry standards vary depending on whether the stone is a diamond or a colored gemstone:

1. For Diamonds (The Global Standards)

GIA (Gemological Institute of America): Widely considered the ultimate gold standard for diamond grading. They created the "4Cs" (Cut, Color, Clarity, Carat) and are globally trusted for strict, unbiased grading.

IGI (International Gemological Institute) & HRD Antwerp: Highly prominent international labs that frequently grade diamonds, lab-grown diamonds, and finished jewelry.

2. For Colored Gemstones (Rubies, Sapphires, Emeralds, etc.)

If you are certifying a colored gemstone, general diamond labs are usually not enough. Collectors and high-end markets rely on specialized colored-stone authorities:

Gübelin Gem Lab (Switzerland): Legendary for high-value colored gemstones, inclusion analysis, and determining geographic origin.

SSEF (Swiss Gemmological Institute): Another elite Swiss lab renowned globally for scientific rigor regarding colored stones, pearls, and origin/treatment detection.

AGL (American Gemological Laboratories): The premier North American authority for colored gemstone grading, treatments, and origin reports.

GRS (GemResearch Swisslab): Widely recognized for evaluating origin and giving trade-accepted color terms (like "pigeon's blood" ruby or "royal blue" sapphire).

How to Verify a Certificate

If a stone comes with a certificate, always check it against the lab's online database (e.g., GIA Report Check or SSEF/Gübelin verification portals). Scammers occasionally forge certificate numbers or match real certificates to fake stones, so scanning the QR code or plugging the report number directly into the official lab website is a critical step.

The Industry-Standard Gemstone Laboratories

When buying colored gemstones online, the value and reliability of a "certification" depend entirely on the issuing laboratory. Unlike diamonds (which follow a strict 4Cs numeric grading scale), colored gemstone reports primarily focus on species identification, detection of treatments (e.g., heating or clarity enhancement), and geographic origin determination.

The most respected laboratories backing online gemstone sales include:

Laboratory	Specialty & Reputation
GIA (Gemological Institute of America)	Globally recognized standard for gem identification, heavily relied upon for sapphires, rubies, and alexandrite.
AGL (American Gemological Laboratories)	Highly respected U.S.-based lab specializing in colored stones, particularly detailed analysis of enhancements and origin.
Gübelin Gem Lab & GRS (GemResearch SwissLab)	Elite Swiss laboratories globally renowned for high-end colored gemstone provenance, origin reports, and treatment disclosures (frequently used for investment-grade rubies, emeralds, and sapphires).
IGI (International Gemological Institute)	Widely used for both colored diamonds and colored gemstone identification reports.

Tips for Buying Certified Gemstones Online

Check the Report Number: Legitimate online jewelers will list the specific certificate or report number on the product page.

Verify Independently: Always take the report number and cross-reference it directly on the issuing laboratory's online database (e.g., GIA Report Check) to confirm the stone matches the digital record.

Understand Treatments: Colored gemstone reports will explicitly state whether a stone is unheated/untreated or if it has undergone enhancements (like heat treatment or fracture filling), which heavily impacts the stone's market value.

Before entering your payment details, run through these critical checks to protect your money:

1. Check for Red Flags Immediately

Vague Product Details: A legitimate £2,000 ring should have precise specifications. Look for the exact gold/platinum carat weight (e.g., 18ct), the specific gemstone type (natural vs. lab-grown), and independent grading reports (like GIA, IGI, or AGS) for valuable stones. If the listing just says "gold ring" or "real gemstone" without details, walk away.

Contact & Business Info: Does the site list a real physical address, a working customer service phone number, and a professional email domain (not a Gmail or Outlook address)?

Prices That Seem Too Good to Be True: If a high-carat gemstone ring is priced drastically lower than market value, it is likely a scam or a synthetic/cubic zirconia substitute.

2. Research the Independent Reputation

Search Outside the Site: Do a web search for the company name alongside words like "reviews," "scam," or "complaints". Check independent review platforms like Trustpilot or Google Reviews. If there is zero trace of the company anywhere else on the internet, do not buy from them.

Check Domain Age: You can use a free tool like WHOIS lookup to see how long their website has been registered. If the domain was created a few weeks or months ago, it's a massive warning sign.

3. Review Policies and Buyer Protection

Return & Refund Policy: High-end jewelry purchases should always come with a clear return window (e.g., 14 to 30 days) and insured return shipping. Check if they charge heavy restocking fees.

Use Secure Payment Methods: Never pay via direct bank transfer, wire, cryptocurrency, or peer-to-peer cash apps for an unknown site. Always use a credit card or a protected platform like PayPal, which gives you chargeback and buyer protection rights if the item never arrives or is completely fraudulent.

If you cannot verify the business's physical existence, find independent reviews, or see clear gemological certifications, it is safer to keep your £2,000 with a reputable, established jeweller.
